Let
\[
S_k=\mathbb P(X_1=\cdots=X_k)=\mathbb E\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^3 Q_i^k\right).
\]
We are given \(S_2=\frac12\) and \(S_3=\frac{11}{36}\), and want the range of \(S_5\).

For \(q=(q_1,q_2,q_3)\), define
\[
r=q_1q_2+q_1q_3+q_2q_3,\qquad s=q_1q_2q_3.
\]
Since \(q_1+q_2+q_3=1\),
\[
\sum q_i^2=1-2r,
\]
so \(\mathbb E r=\frac14\). Also
\[
\sum q_i^3=1-3r+3s,
\]
so
\[
\frac{11}{36}=1-3\cdot\frac14+3\mathbb E s
\]
and therefore
\[
\mathbb E s=\frac1{54}.
\]

Now
\[
\sum q_i^5=1-5r+5r^2+5s-5rs.
\]

For the lower bound, for every \(x\in[0,1]\),
\[
x^5-\left(\frac{67}{36}x^3-\frac{145}{108}x^2+\frac{8}{27}x-\frac5{243}\right)
=
\left(x+\frac53\right)\left(x-\frac16\right)^2\left(x-\frac23\right)^2\ge 0.
\]
Summing over \(x=q_1,q_2,q_3\) and taking expectations gives
\[
S_5\ge
\frac{67}{36}S_3-\frac{145}{108}S_2+\frac{8}{27}\cdot 1-\frac{15}{243}
=\frac{19}{144}.
\]
Equality occurs when \(Q=(2/3,1/6,1/6)\) up to permutation, since then \(S_2=\frac12\), \(S_3=\frac{11}{36}\), and \(S_5=\frac{19}{144}\).

For the upper bound, one has pointwise
\[
\sum q_i^5\le 1-\frac{15}{4}r+\frac{85}{12}s.
\]
Indeed, subtracting the left side from the right gives
\[
5\left(r\left(\frac14-r\right)+s\left(r+\frac5{12}\right)\right)\ge0.
\]
If \(r\le\frac14\), this is immediate. If \(r>\frac14\), minimizing \(s\) at fixed \(r\) occurs when two coordinates are equal; writing \(q=(u,u,1-2u)\), \(u\in[1/3,1/2]\), the bracket becomes
\[
6u\left(u-\frac12\right)\left(u-\frac13\right)^2\left(u-\frac32\right)\ge0.
\]
Thus
\[
S_5\le 1-\frac{15}{4}\cdot\frac14+\frac{85}{12}\cdot\frac1{54}
=\frac{251}{1296}.
\]
Equality is attained by taking
\[
Q=\begin{cases}
(1,0,0),&\text{with probability }1/6,\\
(1/3,1/3,1/3),&\text{with probability }1/2,\\
(1/2,1/2,0),&\text{with probability }1/3.
\end{cases}
\]
This gives the required \(S_2,S_3\), and \(S_5=\frac{251}{1296}\).

Therefore the exact interval is
\[
\boxed{\left[\frac{19}{144},\frac{251}{1296}\right]}.
\]
